title: The $5 Alphonso: Inside the Mango Vans Rolling Through America's Indian Neighbourhoods
excerpt: India's mango exports to the US have already surpassed last year's full-season total, driven by WhatsApp-coordinated delivery vans, surging diaspora demand, and a season extended by northern Indian varieties.
body:
Every summer, the arrival of Indian mangoes in the United States sets off a quiet frenzy in diaspora neighbourhoods. This year, the frenzy is anything but quiet.

In suburban New Jersey, delivery vans loaded with crates of Alphonso, Kesar, and Himayat mangoes pull into apartment complexes and residential streets, their arrival announced not by any advertisement but by WhatsApp messages. Residents gather at designated spots within hours of a notification, purchasing fresh shipments directly from the vehicles. It is a distribution model that owes more to Mumbai's dabbawalas than to Amazon — informal, personal, and built on trust within tightly knit diaspora communities.

## Record-Breaking Numbers

The numbers behind this summer's mango season tell a striking story. India's mango exports to the United States have already surpassed the entire 2025 tally of 2,188 metric tonnes — worth $9.6 million — by the third week of June 2026, according to data cited by *The Economic Times*. Abhishek Dev, chairman of the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), has projected a year-on-year increase of more than 30 per cent this season.

That growth comes despite sharply higher logistics costs. Air cargo rates have escalated significantly following the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran crisis earlier this year, with air freight costs for mangoes roughly tripling at peak. Yet demand has proved remarkably inelastic — when it comes to the king of fruits, the diaspora is willing to pay.

At a typical Indian grocery store in New Jersey, a single mango that retails for roughly 70 cents in India now sells for around $5. A BBC report documented importers like Yakin Shah and Bharat Kumar Parasana in New Jersey spending upwards of $1 million per season on mango imports, with the fruit moving through a network of WhatsApp groups, direct-to-neighbourhood delivery runs, and word-of-mouth within South Asian communities.

## A Broader Export Push

The surge extends well beyond the United States. India's mango exports now reach more than 45 countries, and APEDA has launched promotional campaigns in Seattle, Los Angeles, Washington, New York, and Atlanta to boost visibility among mainstream American consumers. Similar events have been held in nearly 20 countries, from the Czech Republic to Oman.

The extended shipping season is another factor. High-quality varieties from northern India — including Langra, Chausa, and Dashehari — are expected to continue arriving in US markets through July, keeping the export window open weeks longer than in previous years. Dev has said he expects India's overall mango exports to double within two years on the back of this expanded outreach.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For millions of NRIs, the annual mango season is more than a fruit purchase — it is a ritual of homecoming. The specific variety one craves — Alphonso for Maharashtrians, Kesar for Gujaratis, Himayat for Hyderabadis — is a marker of regional identity that transcends geography. Importers have sharpened their offerings to cater to these preferences, recognising that the diaspora market is not monolithic.

The informal delivery networks speak to something else entirely: the entrepreneurial energy of immigrant communities building parallel supply chains that the formal retail system has been slow to serve. When a WhatsApp message can sell a van's worth of mangoes in two hours, it suggests that the demand was always there — it just needed the right channel.

## What's Next

Whether this season's momentum translates into permanent infrastructure — cold storage facilities, dedicated import partnerships, year-round availability of Indian mango products — remains to be seen. But the trajectory is clear: Indian mangoes are no longer a niche luxury in America. They are becoming a summer staple for a diaspora community that is larger, wealthier, and more connected than ever before.

For now, the WhatsApp notifications keep pinging across Edison, Fremont, and Plano. The vans keep rolling. And the $5 Alphonso — improbably expensive by Indian standards, irresistibly cheap by the measure of nostalgia — keeps finding its way home.
